why.correct: pH = −log(3.2 × 10⁻⁴) = 3.495. The concentration has two significant figures, so the pH gets two decimal places: 3.49.
pOH = −log(2.5 × 10⁻³) = 2.602; pH = 14.00 − 2.60 = 11.40. Two significant figures in [OH⁻] give two decimal places.
[H₃O⁺] = 10^−pH = 10^−9.15 = 7.08 × 10⁻¹⁰ M, which is 7.1 × 10⁻¹⁰ M: a pH with two decimal places gives two significant figures.
Convert each to pH: A 3.49, B 11.40, C 9.15, D 14.00 − 11.62 = 2.38. The lowest pH, D, has the most H₃O⁺.
options: Right: a large pOH means little OH⁻, so pH = 2.38, the lowest of the four.
Solution A is acidic (pH 3.49), but D's pH of 2.38 is lower, so D has more H₃O⁺. A was the only one stated as [H₃O⁺], which is not the same as having the most.
This reads [OH⁻] as if it were [H₃O⁺]. A large [OH⁻] means a basic solution, pH 11.40, with very little H₃O⁺.
A larger pH number means less H₃O⁺, not more: pH 9.15 is basic.

why.correct: The pH values differ by 3.49 − 2.38 = 1.11, and each pH unit is a factor of 10, so the ratio is 10^1.11 ≈ 13.
options: Right: a pH difference of 1.11 is a factor of 10^1.11 in [H₃O⁺].
Dividing one pH by the other treats pH as a concentration. pH is a logarithm, so differences, not ratios, carry the meaning.
This is the pH difference itself. The difference is an exponent: raise 10 to it.
That would be a pH difference of about 2.1, one unit too many.

why.correct: A solution is basic when [OH⁻] > [H₃O⁺]. Only Box 3 has more hydroxide (4) than hydronium (1).
options: Right: 4 OH⁻ to 1 H₃O⁺.
Box 1 has equal numbers of the two ions, so it is neutral.
Box 2 has more H₃O⁺ than OH⁻, so it is acidic.
Box 4 has equal numbers of the two ions, so it is neutral even though it holds more ions than Box 1.

why.correct: Each box has 2 × 2 = 4 × 1 = 1 × 4 = 4. This mirrors Kw = [H₃O⁺][OH⁻], which has one value at a given temperature: more H₃O⁺ means less OH⁻.
options: Right: the product is the model of Kw.
The totals differ: 4, 5 and 5 ions. It is the product that stays the same.
Box 2 has fewer OH⁻ than Box 1. Added H₃O⁺ reacts with OH⁻, which lowers [OH⁻].
The boxes have different [H₃O⁺], so different pH values; only the product is the same.

why.correct: Box 4 has a larger ion product (3 × 3 = 9 vs 2 × 2 = 4), so Kw is larger there. 2 H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + OH⁻ absorbs heat, so a higher temperature shifts it toward the ions and raises Kw.
options: Right: Kw grows with temperature because ionization is endothermic.
The reverse: raising the temperature favors the endothermic ionization, so warmer water has more ions.
Box 4 has equal H₃O⁺ and OH⁻, so it is neutral. Acidic means [H₃O⁺] > [OH⁻], not "more H₃O⁺ than another sample".
Box 4 also has more H₃O⁺, so its pH is lower than Box 1, not higher.

why.correct: Box 2 has twice as many H₃O⁺ ions as Box 1 in the same volume, so [H₃O⁺] = 2 × 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ = 2.0 × 10⁻⁷ M. pH = −log(2.0 × 10⁻⁷) = 6.699, or 6.70.
In pure water [H₃O⁺] = [OH⁻] = x, so x² = Kw and x = √(5.5 × 10⁻¹⁴) = 2.35 × 10⁻⁷ M. pH = −log(2.35 × 10⁻⁷) = 6.630, or 6.63.
Neutral means [H₃O⁺] = [OH⁻]. Pure water makes the two ions one for one, so it is neutral at every temperature; only at 25 °C does neutral fall at pH 7.00.
options: Right: the definition is about the two concentrations, not the number 7.
pH 7 marks neutral only at 25 °C. At 50 °C Kw is larger, so neutral water has a lower pH.
Each ionization makes one H₃O⁺ and one OH⁻, so heating raises both equally.
A reading of 6.63 matches √Kw at 50 °C; the meter is behaving correctly.

why.correct: K grows with temperature, so heating shifts the equilibrium toward the ions. By Le Châtelier's principle, heating favors the endothermic direction, so the forward reaction absorbs heat.
options: Right: larger K at higher T means the forward direction absorbs heat.
Heating favors the endothermic direction; if the forward reaction released heat, K would fall as the water warms.
If heating favored the reverse reaction, Kw would fall with temperature; it rises.
Kw is still tiny at 50 °C: only a minute fraction of water molecules are ionized.

why.correct: Cooling favors the exothermic reverse reaction, so both ion concentrations fall together and the water stays neutral at a higher pH.

variables.name: [H₃O⁺]
variables.why: Kw falls from 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ to 1.1 × 10⁻¹⁵, so fewer water molecules are ionized.

variables.name: pH
variables.why: Less H₃O⁺ means a higher pH: neutral water at 0 °C has a pH near 7.5.

variables.name: The ratio [H₃O⁺] / [OH⁻]
variables.why: Each ionization makes one of each ion, so in pure water the ratio stays 1 at every temperature.

variables.name: [OH⁻]
variables.why: Hydroxide falls along with hydronium; they are made together.

why.correct: Two pH units apart is a factor of 10² = 100, and the lower pH has more H₃O⁺.
options: Right: each pH unit is a factor of ten.
This subtracts the pH values and treats the result as a ratio. The difference is an exponent: 10².
This divides 6 by 4. pH values are logarithms, so their ratio has no meaning.
The direction is reversed: a lower pH means more H₃O⁺.

why.correct: pOH first, then pH = 14.00 − pOH, then round once, then sanity-check the side of 7. (Kw / [OH⁻] then −log works too.)
0.0050 has two significant figures, so the pH gets two decimal places: −log(0.0050) = 2.3010 → 2.30. The digits before the decimal point only give the power of ten.
options: Right: two significant figures, two decimal places.
One decimal place throws away a measured digit: 0.0050 has two significant figures.
Three decimal places claim more precision than the two significant figures measured.
Four decimal places treat the trailing zero of 2.3010 as measured, which it is not.

why.correct: Kw holds in every water solution at 25 °C, and taking −log of both sides gives pH + pOH = 14.00. Both ions are present in every solution, in small amounts if not large.
options: Right: Kw applies to any water solution at 25 °C.
At pH 9, [H₃O⁺] = 1 × 10⁻⁹ M: small, but not zero.
Right: −log of Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ gives 14.00.
Added OH⁻ reacts with H₃O⁺, so [H₃O⁺] falls.
An acidic solution still has some OH⁻: [OH⁻] = Kw / [H₃O⁺].

why.correct: HNO₃ ionizes fully, so [H₃O⁺] = 0.0250 M. pH = −log(0.0250) = 1.6021, which is 1.602: three significant figures in the concentration give three decimal places.
The highest pH goes with the highest [OH⁻]. Bottle 2 has 0.0300 M OH⁻ (pH 12.48); Bottle 3 has 0.0040 M (pH 11.60).
options: Right: two OH⁻ per formula unit makes its [OH⁻] the largest.
KOH gives one OH⁻ per formula unit, so [OH⁻] = 0.0040 M, less than Bottle 2's 0.0300 M.
A very dilute HCl solution is still slightly acidic; its pH is just under 7, not 8.
Bottle 1 is an acid, so its pH is the lowest of the four.

why.correct: Water supplies H₃O⁺ too. With x = [OH⁻] from water: [H₃O⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻⁸ + x and (1.0 × 10⁻⁸ + x)(x) = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴. Solving the quadratic gives [H₃O⁺] = 1.05 × 10⁻⁷ M, so pH = 6.98, slightly acidic as an acid solution must be.
Diluting tenfold makes [H₃O⁺] ten times smaller, 0.00250 M, so the pH goes from 1.602 to 2.602: up by exactly log 10 = 1.00.
options: Right: one factor of ten is one pH unit.
Less H₃O⁺ per liter means a higher pH, not a lower one.
A factor of 10 in concentration is one pH unit, because pH is a log scale.
pH depends on concentration, not on the number of moles; the same moles in more water give a lower [H₃O⁺].

why.correct: HCl: 0.0250 L × 0.120 mol/L = 0.00300 mol H₃O⁺. NaOH: 0.0150 L × 0.150 mol/L = 0.00225 mol OH⁻. They react 1:1, leaving 0.00300 − 0.00225 = 7.5 × 10⁻⁴ mol H₃O⁺. Both amounts are known to the 0.00001 mol place, so the difference, 0.00075 mol, has two significant figures.
[H₃O⁺] = 7.5 × 10⁻⁴ mol / 0.0400 L = 0.0188 M. pH = −log(0.0188) = 1.727, which is 1.73 (two significant figures in the leftover moles).
Moles OH⁻ needed = moles HCl = 0.00300 mol; 0.00300 mol ÷ 0.150 mol/L = 0.0200 L = 20.0 mL.
options: Right: equal moles of OH⁻ and H₃O⁺.
That is the volume already added; it leaves acid over.
Equal volumes would be right only if the two concentrations were equal.
This multiplies by the ratio of concentrations the wrong way round: 25.0 × 0.150 / 0.120.

why.correct: At equivalence the flask holds water, Na⁺ and Cl⁻. Neither ion takes a proton from water or gives one to it, so [H₃O⁺] = [OH⁻] and the pH is 7.00 at 25 °C.
options: Right: both are spectator ions, so the solution is neutral.
The order of mixing does not matter: equal moles of H₃O⁺ and OH⁻ have canceled.
At equivalence there is no excess NaOH, whatever was added last.
Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are still dissolved; they just do not change the pH.

why.correct: Five HCl give 5 H₃O⁺ and 5 Cl⁻; three NaOH give 3 Na⁺ and 3 OH⁻. Three H₃O⁺ react with the three OH⁻, leaving 2 H₃O⁺, 5 Cl⁻ and 3 Na⁺: Box W.
options: Right: 2 H₃O⁺ left over, and the spectator ions keep their counts.
Box X is the equivalence point: equal numbers of acid and base.
Box Y has excess OH⁻, which needs more NaOH than HCl.
H₃O⁺ and OH⁻ cannot stay side by side in these amounts: they react until one is used up.

why.correct: Kw = [H₃O⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ is tiny, so large amounts of both ions cannot coexist. They react to make water until the product falls to Kw.
options: Right: neutralization goes essentially to completion.
Na⁺ and Cl⁻ conduct electricity on their own; X is a neutral salt solution.
Excess NaOH gives more Na⁺ than Cl⁻; Y is a real mixture with base left over.
Excess HCl gives more Cl⁻ than Na⁺; W is a real mixture with acid left over.

why.correct: Only Y has excess OH⁻, so it is basic, with the highest pH.
options: Right: excess hydroxide makes it basic.
X is neutral, pH 7 at 25 °C.
W has excess H₃O⁺, so it is acidic.
Z is not a possible mixture.

why.correct: Only HBr is on the list of common strong acids (HCl, HBr, HI, HNO₃, HClO₄, H₂SO₄ for its first proton). Select-all items can have a single answer.
options: Right: a hydrohalic strong acid.
HF is the one hydrohalic acid that does not ionize fully in water.
Nitrous acid, HNO₂, is weak; it is nitric acid, HNO₃, that is strong.
Carbonic acid ionizes only slightly.
Acetic acid (vinegar) ionizes only slightly.

why.correct: For a strong acid, [H₃O⁺] equals the acid concentration, whatever the acid. The anion (Cl⁻ or NO₃⁻) is a spectator.
options: Right: full ionization makes the pH depend on concentration alone.
The molar masses differ (36.46 and 63.01 g/mol); the solutions are compared in mol/L anyway.
The two electronegativities are close but the structures differ. What matters here is that both ionize fully.
HNO₃ is not diatomic. Each acid gives one proton per molecule, but that alone does not explain equal pH unless both ionize fully.

why.correct: Moles first, because acid and base react by moles, not by concentration. Then the excess, then the total volume, then the log.
Ka = x² / (0.20 − x) = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵. Assume x ≪ 0.20: x = √(1.8 × 10⁻⁵ × 0.20) = 1.90 × 10⁻³ M = [H₃O⁺]. Check: 0.9% of 0.20, under 5%, so the assumption holds. pH = −log(1.9 × 10⁻³) = 2.72.
At equal concentration, the acid with the smallest Ka ionizes least, makes the least H₃O⁺ and so has the highest pH. HOCl has Ka = 3.0 × 10⁻⁸.
options: Right: the smallest Ka, the least H₃O⁺.
HF has the largest Ka here, so it gives the most H₃O⁺ and the lowest pH.
HNO₂ has the second-largest Ka, so its pH is low.
Acetic acid ionizes more than HOCl (Ka 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ vs 3.0 × 10⁻⁸), so its pH is lower.

why.correct: Small x gives x = √(4.0 × 10⁻⁴ × 0.050) = 4.47 × 10⁻³ M, which is 8.9% of 0.050: over 5%, so solve x² + (4.0 × 10⁻⁴)x − 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ = 0. x = 4.28 × 10⁻³ M. Percent ionization = x / 0.050 × 100 = 8.6%.
F⁻ is the conjugate base of HF. Ka × Kb = Kw, so Kb = (1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴) / (6.8 × 10⁻⁴) = 1.5 × 10⁻¹¹.
Kb = Kw / Ka, so the weakest acid has the strongest conjugate base. HOCl has the smallest Ka, so OCl⁻ has the largest Kb (about 3.3 × 10⁻⁷).
options: Right: smallest Ka, largest Kb.
This assumes a strong acid has a strong conjugate base. It is the reverse: HF has the largest Ka, so F⁻ has the smallest Kb.
HNO₂ has a large Ka, so NO₂⁻ is a weak base.
Acetate is a stronger base than F⁻ or NO₂⁻, but HOCl is a weaker acid than acetic acid, so OCl⁻ is stronger still.

why.correct: A strong acid ionizes fully, so no HA molecules remain. Only Box 2 has none.
options: Right: only ions, no whole molecules.
Box 1 is mostly whole HA molecules: a weak acid.
Box 3 still has whole HA molecules: a weak acid.
The particle view is enough: a strong acid leaves no whole HA molecules, and only Box 2 has none.

why.correct: Box 1: 1 of 7 acid particles ionized (14%); Box 3: 1 of 4 (25%), with fewer acid particles in the same volume, so it is more dilute. Diluting a weak acid raises its percent ionization: Q = [H₃O⁺][A⁻]/[HA] falls below Ka on dilution, so more HA ionizes.
options: Right: fewer particles per volume, a larger fraction ionized.
Ka is fixed for an acid at a given temperature; it does not change with concentration.
Both have one H₃O⁺ in the same volume, so the same pH. Whole HA molecules do not lower the pH.
Percent ionization depends on concentration as well as on the acid.
Right: equilibrium concentrations of both products over the reactant.
This leaves out one product: Ka has [H₃O⁺] and [A⁻] in the numerator.
This uses the starting amount of HA (7 particles), not the 6 left at equilibrium.
This leaves out the denominator [HA].

why.correct: Six whole molecules against one ionized: [HA] > [A⁻], and the acid is mostly un-ionized, which is what makes it weak.
options: Right: 6 HA to 1 A⁻.
That is true of a strong acid. Here [H₃O⁺] is only 1/7 of the acid added.
Right: the defining feature of a weak acid.
Dilution raises the percent ionization of a weak acid.

why.correct: Kb = x² / (0.15 − x) ≈ x² / 0.15, so x = √(1.8 × 10⁻⁵ × 0.15) = 1.64 × 10⁻³ M = [OH⁻] (1.1% of 0.15, so the approximation holds). Rounded: 1.6 × 10⁻³ M.
pOH = −log(1.64 × 10⁻³) = 2.784; pH = 14.00 − 2.784 = 11.216, which is 11.22 (two significant figures in 0.15 M, two decimal places). Solving the quadratic gives 11.21; both are accepted.
pKb = −log(1.8 × 10⁻⁵) = 4.745. pKa + pKb = pKw = 14.00, so pKa = 14.00 − 4.74 = 9.26. (Equivalently Ka = Kw/Kb = 5.6 × 10⁻¹⁰.)
Weak describes the fraction that reacts (about 1% here), not the pH. Even 1% of 0.15 M is 1.6 × 10⁻³ M OH⁻, far above water's 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ M.
options: Right: weak is about extent of reaction, not about being near neutral.
Weak and dilute are different ideas: a 15 M ammonia solution is concentrated and still weak.
NH₃ accepts a proton from water, which leaves OH⁻; the solution is basic.
Reacting fully would make it a strong base.

why.correct: Equation and expression, ICE table, small-x estimate, the 5% check, then the log. The check comes before you trust x.

HCl ionizes fully, so [H₃O⁺] falls tenfold and pH rises by 1.0. For HF, dilution makes Q < Ka, so more HF ionizes and partly offsets the dilution: [H₃O⁺] falls only by about √10, and pH rises by about 0.5.
options: Right: dilution raises the percent ionization of the weak acid.
Only the strong acid follows the one-unit rule; the weak acid ionizes more when diluted.
The extra ionization of HF on dilution makes its pH rise less, not more.
K values stay the same, but concentrations change, so pH changes.

why.correct: Weak means the ionization equilibrium lies to the left (Ka ≪ 1): most molecules stay as HA. Stating "Ka < 1, mostly un-ionized" is what readers look for, not just "weak Ka".
options: Right: small Ka, mostly un-ionized.
Any acid solution has a pH below 7.
HCl also has one ionizable hydrogen and is strong; the count does not decide strength.
Weak and dilute are different: concentration does not change Ka.

why.correct: Flask 2 has 5.00 × 10⁻³ mol acetic acid and 2.50 × 10⁻³ mol NaOH. The OH⁻ converts half the acid to acetate, leaving equal amounts of CH₃COOH and CH₃COO⁻: a weak acid with its conjugate base.
options: Right: weak acid and conjugate base in similar amounts.
Flask 1 holds only acetic acid; there is no conjugate base to react with added acid.
Flask 3 is exactly neutralized: all the acid became acetate, so there is no weak acid left.
Flask 4 has excess NaOH and no acetic acid left; its pH is set by the strong base.

why.correct: After reaction: 2.50 × 10⁻³ mol CH₃COOH and 2.50 × 10⁻³ mol CH₃COO⁻. In Ka = [H₃O⁺][A⁻]/[HA], the volume cancels, so [H₃O⁺] = Ka × (2.50 × 10⁻³)/(2.50 × 10⁻³) = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ M and pH = −log(1.8 × 10⁻⁵) = 4.74, which is pKa.
All 5.00 × 10⁻³ mol acid became acetate, now in 100.0 mL: [CH₃COO⁻] = 0.0500 M. Kb = Kw/Ka = 5.56 × 10⁻¹⁰. [OH⁻] = √(5.56 × 10⁻¹⁰ × 0.0500) = 5.27 × 10⁻⁶ M; pOH = 5.278; pH = 8.72.
OH⁻ added: 6.00 × 10⁻³ mol; acid: 5.00 × 10⁻³ mol. Excess OH⁻ = 1.00 × 10⁻³ mol in 0.1100 L = 0.00909 M. The acetate adds very little OH⁻ beside this. pOH = 2.041; pH = 11.96.
Every acetic acid molecule reacted with OH⁻, so the flask holds 5.00 × 10⁻³ mol CH₃COO⁻. Only a tiny amount of it takes a proton back from water.
options: Right: the conjugate base is what remains at equivalence.
Only a trace of CH₃COOH re-forms, about 5 × 10⁻⁶ M.
OH⁻ is present at about 5 × 10⁻⁶ M, made by acetate reacting with water; far less than the acetate.
The solution is basic, so H₃O⁺ is the scarcest of these.

why.correct: Box P has a weak acid (HF) and its conjugate base (F⁻) in equal amounts. Added H₃O⁺ reacts with F⁻; added OH⁻ reacts with HF.
options: Right: weak acid plus conjugate base.
Box Q is a strong acid solution with spare Cl⁻. Cl⁻ is too weak a base to remove added H₃O⁺.
Box R has the base F⁻ but no HF to react with added OH⁻.
Box S has the weak acid but no F⁻ to react with added H₃O⁺.

why.correct: HCl ionizes fully, so its conjugate base has a negligible Kb: Cl⁻ does not pick protons back up. Added acid would stay as free H₃O⁺, and the pH would drop sharply.
options: Right: a buffer needs a conjugate base strong enough to react with added acid.
Buffers work over a range of ratios; unequal amounts are not the problem here.
Na⁺ is a spectator ion; it does not react with OH⁻.
Every water solution has some H₃O⁺, buffers included.

why.correct: Box R holds only F⁻, a weak base: F⁻ + H₂O ⇌ HF + OH⁻ makes the solution slightly basic. Every other box contains an acid.
options: Right: the conjugate base alone gives a basic solution.
Box P is a buffer at pH = pKa of HF, about 3.2: acidic.
Box Q is a strong acid solution, the lowest pH of the four.
Box S is HF alone, a weak acid: acidic.

why.correct: OH⁻ + HF → F⁻ + H₂O goes to completion: two HF become two F⁻, and the two Na⁺ added with the OH⁻ stay as spectators.
options: Right: two HF used, two F⁻ made, six Na⁺ in all.
The OH⁻ cannot stay free beside HF: it reacts with the weak acid.
The change goes the wrong way: OH⁻ removes HF and makes F⁻.
This loses two F⁻ and the Na⁺ added with the base; ions are not destroyed.

why.correct: A buffer needs a weak acid and its conjugate base (or a weak base and its conjugate acid) together. HNO₂/NO₂⁻ qualifies directly; NH₃ + half as much HCl leaves 0.10 mol NH₃ and 0.10 mol NH₄⁺.
options: Right: weak acid and conjugate base.
HNO₃ is strong; NO₃⁻ cannot remove added acid.
Right: partial neutralization of a weak base makes NH₃/NH₄⁺.
Equal moles convert all NH₃ to NH₄⁺; no weak base remains.
Strong base and strong acid leave only excess NaOH.

why.correct: HF is weak, so it is mostly molecules and is written whole. NaOH is a strong electrolyte, so it appears as OH⁻ with Na⁺ canceled as a spectator.
options: Right: weak acid written as a molecule.
This is the net equation for a strong acid; HF is not ionized enough to write it as H₃O⁺.
This is the molecular equation; it still shows the spectator Na⁺ inside NaOH and NaF.
This splits HF into ions as if it were strong.

why.correct: HF + H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + F⁻ (Ka) plus H₃O⁺ + OH⁻ ⇌ 2 H₂O (1/Kw) gives the net reaction, so K = Ka/Kw = (6.8 × 10⁻⁴)/(1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴) = 6.8 × 10¹⁰. So large that the reaction goes essentially to completion.
The product NH₄⁺ is the conjugate acid of a weak base: NH₄⁺ + H₂O ⇌ NH₃ + H₃O⁺ (Ka = Kw/Kb = 5.6 × 10⁻¹⁰), so the solution is slightly acidic.
options: Right: the conjugate acid of a weak base is a weak acid.
Equal moles give a neutral solution only for strong acid with strong base.
All the NH₃ was converted to NH₄⁺; no base is left.
Cl⁻ is a spectator, but NH₄⁺ is not: it reacts with water.

why.correct: Added acid converts the weak base into its conjugate acid; the mixture of NH₃ and NH₄⁺ is a buffer.

variables.name: Moles of NH₃
variables.why: H₃O⁺ + NH₃ → NH₄⁺ + H₂O uses up ammonia, one for one with the acid added.

variables.name: Moles of NH₄⁺
variables.why: Each H₃O⁺ that reacts makes one NH₄⁺.

variables.name: Kb of NH₃
variables.why: Kb is an equilibrium constant and changes only with temperature, not with what is added.

variables.name: pH
variables.why: Less base and more of its conjugate acid: the pH falls, though only a little once NH₄⁺ is present.

why.correct: Rearrange Ka = [H₃O⁺][NO₂⁻]/[HNO₂]: [H₃O⁺] = 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ × 0.30/0.20 = 6.0 × 10⁻⁴ M. pH = −log(6.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 3.22. Both amounts barely change, because the NO₂⁻ already present pushes the ionization of HNO₂ even further left.
Half of 0.0400 mol is 0.0200 mol; 0.0200 mol ÷ 0.500 mol/L = 0.0400 L = 40.0 mL. The flask then holds 0.0200 mol each of acid and acetate.

H₃O⁺ + NH₃ → NH₄⁺ leaves 0.010 mol NH₃ and 0.010 mol NH₄⁺. For NH₄⁺, Ka = Kw/Kb = 5.6 × 10⁻¹⁰. [H₃O⁺] = Ka × [NH₄⁺]/[NH₃] = 5.56 × 10⁻¹⁰ × 1 = 5.56 × 10⁻¹⁰ M → pH = 9.26 (rounding Ka to 5.6 × 10⁻¹⁰ first gives 9.25, also accepted).
All the HCN becomes CN⁻, the conjugate base of a very weak acid. CN⁻ + H₂O ⇌ HCN + OH⁻ (Kb = 1.6 × 10⁻⁵) makes the solution basic.
options: Right: a weak acid neutralized by a strong base leaves a basic solution.
Equal moles give pH 7 only when both are strong.
No HCN remains after it reacts with an equal amount of KOH.
K⁺ is a spectator, but CN⁻ is not.

why.correct: The neutralization runs first because its K is huge. What remains decides which equilibrium sets the pH.
Added acid is taken up by the base of the pair, NH₃, which becomes NH₄⁺. Free H₃O⁺ stays low.
options: Right: the weak base removes the added acid.
NH₄⁺ already carries a positive charge and has no lone pair to accept another proton.
This is how the buffer handles added base, not added acid.
Cl⁻ is the conjugate base of a strong acid and does not take protons.

why.correct: At equivalence, mol OH⁻ = mol HA: 0.02000 L × 0.100 mol/L = 2.00 × 10⁻³ mol. [HA] = 2.00 × 10⁻³ mol / 0.02500 L = 0.0800 M.
At the half-equivalence point (half of 20.00 mL), half the HA has become A⁻, so [HA] = [A⁻]. In Ka = [H₃O⁺][A⁻]/[HA] the two cancel: Ka = [H₃O⁺], so pH = pKa.
options: Right: half-equivalence, where [HA] = [A⁻].
This is the equivalence point, where no HA is left; its pH is set by A⁻ acting as a base. Confusing equivalence with half-equivalence is the most common titration error.
At the start no A⁻ has been made, so [HA] ≠ [A⁻].
Past equivalence the pH is set by excess OH⁻.

why.correct: Adding water does not change the moles of HA, so the same 2.00 × 10⁻³ mol of OH⁻ (20.00 mL) reaches equivalence. At half-equivalence [HA] = [A⁻] still, so pH = pKa again.
options: Right: moles of acid set the equivalence volume; the ratio at half-equivalence is unchanged.
The equivalence volume depends on moles of acid, not on the volume the acid is dissolved in.
The moles of acid are the same, so the base needed is the same.
pH = pKa at half-equivalence whatever the dilution, because [HA]/[A⁻] = 1.

why.correct: At equivalence, base added equals acid present: all 6 HA became 6 A⁻, with 6 Na⁺ from the 6 NaOH, and no OH⁻ left over.
options: Right: only A⁻ and Na⁺.
Box W is the half-equivalence point: half the HA has been converted.
Box X is the start: no base added yet.
Box Y is past equivalence: 2 extra OH⁻.

why.correct: [HA] = [A⁻] (3 and 3), so in Ka = [H₃O⁺][A⁻]/[HA] the ratio is 1 and [H₃O⁺] = Ka.
options: Right: equal amounts of the acid and its conjugate base.
Box Z has no HA left; it is the equivalence point, not the half-equivalence point.
At the start there is no A⁻, so the ratio is not 1.
Past equivalence, excess OH⁻ sets the pH.

why.correct: Start (only HA), half-equivalence (equal HA and A⁻), equivalence (only A⁻), then past equivalence (A⁻ plus excess OH⁻). Na⁺ rises as NaOH is added: 0, 3, 6, 8.
A⁻ is a weak base: A⁻ + H₂O ⇌ HA + OH⁻. With no HA or strong acid left, that small amount of OH⁻ makes the solution basic.
options: Right: the conjugate base of a weak acid gives a basic equivalence point.
Equal moles give pH 7 only for strong acid with strong base.
pH = pKa needs equal HA and A⁻; Z has no HA.
All the HA has been converted; the acid is gone.

why.correct: Na⁺ counts the NaOH added: 8 × 5.00 × 10⁻⁴ mol = 4.00 × 10⁻³ mol. Volume = 4.00 × 10⁻³ mol ÷ 0.100 mol/L = 0.0400 L = 40.0 mL. (The pKa is not needed.)
Acetic acid is mostly un-ionized, so its starting pH (2.88) is higher than HCl's (1.00), and at equivalence acetate makes the solution basic (pH 8.72).
options: Right: higher start, basic equivalence point.
A lower pH means more H₃O⁺, not fewer; Acid 1 is the strong acid.
Both need 25.0 mL: equal moles of acid need equal moles of base, whatever their strength.
pH 7 at equivalence is the mark of a strong acid with a strong base.

why.correct: Each flask holds 2.50 × 10⁻³ mol of acid. OH⁻ removes HCl's H₃O⁺ and also takes the proton from acetic acid molecules directly (K = 1.8 × 10⁹), so each needs 2.50 × 10⁻³ mol OH⁻.
options: Right: equivalence counts total acid, ionized or not.
Their starting pH values differ by almost two units.
Before equivalence, acetic acid is still mostly molecules; what matters is that OH⁻ reacts with those molecules.
The equivalence volume depends on the moles of acid present, not only on the base.

why.correct: OH⁻ converts 1.00 × 10⁻³ mol acid to acetate, leaving 1.50 × 10⁻³ mol CH₃COOH. [H₃O⁺] = Ka × [HA]/[A⁻] = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ × 1.50/1.00 = 2.7 × 10⁻⁵ M; pH = 4.57.
The equivalence volume tracks the moles of acid; the half-equivalence pH tracks the acid itself.

variables.name: Volume of NaOH at the equivalence point
variables.why: Twice the moles of acid need twice the moles of OH⁻: 50.0 mL.

variables.name: pH at the half-equivalence point
variables.why: At half-equivalence [HA] = [A⁻] for any starting amount, so pH = pKa = 4.74 again.

variables.name: Starting pH
variables.why: A more concentrated weak acid makes more H₃O⁺: √(Ka·C) grows with C.

why.correct: At half-equivalence [NH₃] = [NH₄⁺]. For the acid of this pair, Ka = [H₃O⁺][NH₃]/[NH₄⁺] = [H₃O⁺], so pH = pKa of NH₄⁺ = 14.00 − pKb = 9.26.
options: Right: half-equivalence gives pKa of the conjugate acid.
pKb is the pOH at half-equivalence, not the pH. Using pKb where pKa of the conjugate acid belongs is a frequent error with weak bases.
That is the pH at equivalence, 25.0 mL.
Half-neutralized ammonia is a basic mixture of NH₃ and NH₄⁺, not a neutral one.

why.correct: At equivalence every NH₃ has been converted to NH₄⁺. A small fraction of NH₄⁺ gives a proton to water, which is why the pH is below 7.
options: Right: the conjugate acid is what remains.
Only a trace of NH₃ re-forms from NH₄⁺.
H₃O⁺ is about 5 × 10⁻⁶ M, far below the 0.0500 M NH₄⁺.
The solution is acidic, so OH⁻ is scarce.

why.correct: Adding HCl lowers the pH, so the curve runs downhill. The equivalence point holds NH₄⁺, a weak acid, so its pH is about 5.3, a mirror of acetate's 8.7.
options: Right: downhill, with an acidic equivalence point.
Excess HCl makes the end of this curve acidic, not basic: the curve goes down.
The two K values match, but one equivalence point holds a weak acid (NH₄⁺) and the other a weak base (CH₃COO⁻).
Ammonia is a weak base, which is why the curve has a buffer region and an acidic equivalence point.

why.correct: A diprotic acid has one equivalence point per proton: H₂A → HA⁻ (first 20.0 mL), then HA⁻ → A²⁻ (next 20.0 mL). Equal volumes, because each step removes the same moles of protons.
options: Right: one equivalence point per ionizable proton.
Two acids could also give two rises, but the equal 20.0 mL steps fit one diprotic acid with 2.00 × 10⁻³ mol of each proton.
A titration curve plots the pH of the flask; refilling a buret does not show up.
A half-equivalence point lies in a flat buffer region, not at a steep rise.

why.correct: Between the first equivalence point (20.0 mL) and the second (40.0 mL), OH⁻ converts HA⁻ to A²⁻. Halfway, at 30.0 mL, [HA⁻] = [A²⁻], so pH = pKa₂.
options: Right: the second half-equivalence point.
That is the second equivalence point, where all HA⁻ has become A²⁻.
That is pKa₁, halfway to the first equivalence point.
That is the first equivalence point, where HA⁻ is the main species.

why.correct: At the first equivalence point exactly one proton per H₂A has been removed: all 2.00 × 10⁻³ mol H₂A has become HA⁻.
options: Right: the first equivalence point holds HA⁻.
H₂A is used up at the first equivalence point.
A²⁻ forms only after 20.0 mL.
No excess OH⁻ is present until after 40.0 mL.

why.correct: At 10.0 mL (first half-equivalence) [H₂A] ≈ [HA⁻] and pH ≈ pKa₁ = 4.0; the second equivalence point is at 40.0 mL, twice (not three times) 20.0 mL.
options: Right: read at 10.0 mL.
pKa₂ (8.5) is larger than pKa₁ (4.0), so Ka₂ is smaller: the second proton comes off a negative ion and is held more tightly.
40.0 mL is twice 20.0 mL: each proton needs the same moles of OH⁻, so the second equivalence point needs twice the NaOH of the first.
Right: half of H₂A converted to HA⁻.
A strong acid would start near pH 1.0 and show no flat region before the first rise.

why.correct: Each region has one equilibrium that controls it. Find which species are left after the neutralization, then pick the matching method.
Water left in the buret dilutes the NaOH, so more volume is delivered to supply the same moles of OH⁻. The student multiplies that larger volume by the labeled molarity and overestimates the acid.
options: Right: larger volume × assumed molarity = too many moles.
The NaOH is diluted, but the calculation uses the labeled molarity, so the error runs the other way.
Water does not change the moles of acid, but it lowers the molarity of the titrant actually used.
Diluted titrant means more volume is needed, not less.

why.correct: One counterexample refutes "any". At the equivalence point of NH₃ with HCl, the flask holds NH₄⁺, a weak acid, so the pH is below 7.
options: Right: a concrete case with a non-7 equivalence pH.
This case agrees with the claim, so it cannot refute it.
True, but it says nothing about the pH.
True, but it does not say what that pH is.

why.correct: Half-equivalence is half the equivalence volume: 32.40 mL ÷ 2 = 16.20 mL. There half the acid has become A⁻, so [HA] = [A⁻] and pH = pKa.

An electron-withdrawing Cl two carbons away draws electron density from the –COO⁻ group, so the negative charge of ClCH₂COO⁻ is less concentrated and the ion is more stable. A more stable conjugate base means a larger Ka.
options: Right: electron withdrawal stabilizes the conjugate base.
The acidic H is still the one on –COOH; Cl replaces a C–H hydrogen, which is not acidic.
Molar mass does not set acid strength; the effect comes from electronegativity.
The C=O bond is still there; Cl changes electron density, not the bonding pattern.

why.correct: F (electronegativity 4.0) pulls harder than Cl (3.2), so FCH₂COO⁻ is more stabilized and FCH₂COOH ionizes more.
options: Right: the stronger the pull, the more stable the anion.
F is smaller than Cl, yet its acid is stronger, so size is not the cause here.
There is no H–F bond: F is bonded to carbon, and the acidic H is on –COOH.
F does not create new resonance forms of the carboxylate; its effect is a pull through the bonds.

why.correct: Each Cl added pulls more electron density from the carboxylate, so Ka rises with every substitution: 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ → 1.4 × 10⁻³ → 5.5 × 10⁻² → larger still for three.
options: Right: three Cl atoms, the largest Ka of the series.
That is the value for two Cl atoms; a third Cl should increase it.
That is the value for one Cl atom.
This would make it weaker than acetic acid, against the trend.

why.correct: Kb = Kw/Ka, so the weakest acid (acetic acid, smallest Ka) has the strongest conjugate base. Its negative charge is the least stabilized, so it holds a proton most readily.
options: Right: smallest Ka, largest Kb.
Chloroacetate is stabilized by the Cl, so it is a weaker base than acetate.
With two Cl atoms its charge is the most spread out: the weakest base here.
Fluoroacetate is stabilized even more than chloroacetate.

why.correct: HOCl and HOBr have the same structure (H–O–X, no extra O), so the only difference is the central atom.
options: Right: same structure, different central atom.
These share the central atom; they isolate the number of O atoms.
These differ in both the central atom and the number of O atoms.
These differ in both the central atom and the number of O atoms.

why.correct: In ClO₂⁻ the negative charge is shared between two O atoms (two resonance forms), and the extra O pulls electron density from the O–H bond. Both make the conjugate base more stable and the acid stronger.
options: Right: more O, a more stable conjugate base.
HOClO has one H, bonded to O; it is monoprotic.
The extra O weakens the O–H bond by pulling electron density away from it.
Electronegativity is a property of the element; Cl is the same atom in both.

why.correct: Ka falls from 3.0 × 10⁻⁸ to 2.0 × 10⁻⁹ to 2.3 × 10⁻¹¹ as the central atom's electronegativity falls from 3.2 to 2.7. A weaker pull leaves more electron density in the O–H bond and on the O of the anion, so the anion is less stable.
options: Right: the Ka data match the electronegativity order.
In oxyacids the H is on O, not on the halogen, so the halogen's size is not the deciding factor; the data show the acids getting weaker.
The O–H bond length barely changes; the trend follows electronegativity.
The Ka values span three powers of ten, so strength is not the same.

why.correct: CH₃COO⁻ has two equivalent resonance structures, each O carrying the charge half the time. CH₃CH₂O⁻ has no such spreading, so it is far less stable and ethanol barely ionizes.
options: Right: resonance delocalizes the charge of the carboxylate.
Only one H, on the –COOH group, is acidic; the C–H hydrogens are not.
Acetic acid is also a liquid at room temperature; the state is not the cause.
Both molecules hydrogen-bond with water.

why.correct: A Brønsted-Lowry base needs a lone pair to bond to H⁺. The N lone pair forms the new N–H bond: CH₃NH₂ + H₂O ⇌ CH₃NH₃⁺ + OH⁻.
options: Right: the nitrogen lone pair.
Carbon has four bonds and no lone pair, so it cannot accept a proton here.
An H atom cannot accept another proton; the new bond forms to N.
The carbon in methylamine has no lone pair.

why.correct: The amine N has a lone pair and is the basic site, so in strong acid it becomes –NH₃⁺. The –COOH group stays un-ionized.
options: Right: the amine nitrogen is the basic site.
A carbon with four bonds has no lone pair to accept H⁺.
Carbon atoms with C–H bonds have no lone pairs.
The –COOH oxygen is not the basic site here; the amine N, with its lone pair, is a far stronger base and takes the proton.

why.correct: Down a group, the central atom gets larger, the bond to H gets longer and weaker, and the negative charge of the anion is spread over a larger volume. So H₂Se gives up H⁺ most readily. (Here bond strength wins over electronegativity, which falls down the group.)
F is a small atom, so the H–F bond is short and strong (567 kJ/mol), and F⁻ holds its charge in a tiny volume. Both oppose giving up H⁺, so HF is the one weak hydrohalic acid.
options: Right: bond strength and the small anion.
F is the most electronegative element.
H–F is very polar; polarity alone would suggest a strong acid, which is why bond strength matters here.
F⁻ is the conjugate base of a weak acid; that is the point to explain.

why.correct: Across a period the atoms are similar in size, so electronegativity wins: a more electronegative atom makes the X–H bond more polar and holds the negative charge of X⁻ more easily.
options: Right: electronegativity rises from C to F.
Fewer H atoms do not cause a stronger acid; this is a coincidence of these formulas.
Across a period, atoms get slightly smaller, not larger.
Molar mass barely changes and is not the cause.

why.correct: Anything that stabilizes A⁻ (spreading its charge by resonance or pulling electron density with an electronegative atom) shifts HA + H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + A⁻ to the right.
options: Right: delocalized charge, a more stable anion.
Right: electron withdrawal stabilizes A⁻.
C is less electronegative than O; C–H bonds are far less acidic.
A less stable conjugate base means a weaker acid.
